name: main
prose: Entry point of lock (usr.bin/lock/lock.c:81-255). Options: -t minutes (errx(1) if atoi gives <= 0), -p (use the user's own PAM authentication; errx(1) if getpwuid fails), -n (no timeout), -v (lock the vty), anything else calls usage() (exit 1). Without -p it drops privileges with setuid(getuid()) (errx(1) on failure). It then exit(1)s if tcgetattr on fd 0 fails, errx(1) if ttyname(0) fails, records the time, installs quit for SIGINT/SIGQUIT and turns terminal echo off. With -p it calls pam_start; failure is err(1) and the process exits with echo still off (the terminal is not restored there). Without -p it prompts twice for a key: if the first fgets fails or the line is just a newline it calls quit(0); if the two keys differ it prints a message, restores the terminal and exit(1). It then installs hi for SIGINT/SIGQUIT/SIGTSTP and bye for SIGALRM, starts the interval timer unless -n, and with -v issues the VT_LOCKSWITCH ioctl (on failure it restores the terminal and err(1)). It prints the lock banner and loops: with -p it calls pam_authenticate, leaving the loop on PAM_SUCCESS and otherwise (logging unexpected errors to syslog) going to the tryagain code; without -p it reads a key (on read failure it clears stdin's error, calls hi(0) and goes to tryagain) and leaves the loop if it equals the stored key; each wrong key counts a failure (syslogged when root) and the loop then calls tcgetattr, which exit(1)s on failure other than EINTR (without restoring the terminal), sleeps one second and repeats. After the loop it syslogs a root unlock, calls pam_end with -p and calls quit(0), which restores the terminal attributes, unlocks the vty if locked and exit(0)s. The function does not return normally. The signal handlers can end the process too: bye (SIGALRM, only when a timeout is on) restores the terminal and exit(1)s; hi only prints.
note: usr.bin/lock/lock.c:81-255; pam_start err at 151-153 (no tcsetattr restore), key mismatch 166-170, VT ioctl 191-194, loop 215-247, tcgetattr 244-245 (exit only if errno != EINTR), quit 281-289, bye 291-301. Reviewer round 1 right (pam_start failure exits with echo still off); round 15 right (EINTR tcgetattr failure continues). tryagain label is at line 243 just before the tcgetattr call, so the pam and read-failure paths skip the failure count.

name: main
prose: Entry point of login (usr.bin/login/login.c:155-667; slice cut the head). It ignores SIGQUIT/SIGINT/SIGHUP, sets a SIGALRM timeout handler (via setjmp/longjmp: on timeout it logs a failed attempt if any, prints 'Login timed out' and calls bail(NO_SLEEP_EXIT, 0), exit status 0), parses -f, -h host (errx(1) unless root or if the name is too long), -p; other options call usage(). A user name operand is copied with strdup (err(1) on failure). It closes descriptors from 3, finds the tty name with ttyname(0) (a '??' name under _PATH_TTY is used if that fails, so stdin need not be a tty), reads login class parameters, then loops: asks for the name if needed, runs pam_start/pam_set_item (failure: pam_syslog and bail(NO_SLEEP_EXIT, 1)), looks the user up, and either accepts -f for root or the same user or calls auth_pam(); a success with a valid passwd entry leaves the loop; otherwise it prints 'Login incorrect', counts failures and, after the backoff count, sleeps or, at the retry limit, calls badlogin and bail(SLEEP_EXIT, 1). After success it cancels the alarm, installs bail_sig for SIGHUP/SIGTERM, calls pam_setcred (failure: bail(NO_SLEEP_EXIT, 1)), changes to the home directory (refused()/bail if requirehome or the root directory is unusable, else falls back to '/'), picks the shell with strdup (bail(SLEEP_EXIT, 1) on failure), fixes tty ownership, builds the environment, calls setusercontext (bail(NO_SLEEP_EXIT, 1) on failure), pam_setcred reinitialise and pam_open_session (bail(NO_SLEEP_EXIT, 1) on failure) and forks. fork failure is err(1). The parent waits for the child and then calls bail(NO_SLEEP_EXIT, 0), exiting with status 0. The child does export_pam_environment, pam_end, setlogin (bail(NO_SLEEP_EXIT, 1) on failure), the rest of setusercontext (plain exit(1) on failure), sets environment variables, prints the motd and mail notice unless quiet, resets signals, builds arg0 (errx(1) if the shell path is too long, err(1) if asprintf fails) and calls execlp(shell, arg0, NULL); if that returns it calls err(1). bail/bail_internal run pam_cleanup (closing any established session and credentials), sleep the requested seconds and exit(eval). Main never returns.
note: usr.bin/login/login.c:155-667; timeout 184-190 (bail(NO_SLEEP_EXIT, 0)), fork 548-567 (parent bail(..., 0) at 566), execlp 661-662; bail_internal 991-1015. Reviewer round 15 right (timeout exits 0); round 1 right (stdin tty not required, some failures exit via errx/err/usage rather than bail). Partly read: auth_pam, refused, getloginname, badlogin and export_pam_environment not read.

name: macro
prose: Main m4 input loop (usr.bin/m4/main.c:350-521; returns nothing). It reads characters with gpbc() in an endless loop and handles: an opening quote (nested quotes are counted; the quote delimiters are stripped except nested ones, and the text goes directly to the output when not inside a macro call (sp < 0) or is saved on the string stack otherwise; end of input inside the quote prints 'unclosed quote' (with the count) via warnx, dumps the quote stack and calls exit(1)); a comment start when not inside a macro (copied through to the end delimiter or EOF); an identifier, looked up with inspect(): if it is not a macro, or is a macro needing arguments that is not followed by '(', its name is output (to the string stack when sp >= 0), otherwise a call frame is pushed and, with no '(' and parenthesis level 0, the macro is evaluated immediately with eval(), and sp, fp and ep are restored to their earlier values; an overflow of the macro stack there or later is errx(1, "internal stack overflow") with no stack dump; EOF: if not mimic_gnu and a macro call is still open at the top input level (sp > -1 and ilevel <= 0) it warns 'unexpected end of input, unclosed parenthesis', dumps the paren stack and exit(1)s; otherwise at the top level (ilevel <= 0) the loop ends and the function returns, and at a nested input level the input is released and the loop continues; any other character is output directly when sp < 0, and inside a macro call '(' , ')' and ',' manage argument collection (')' at level 0 evaluates the call and restores sp/fp/ep) and other characters, including comments, are saved on the string stack. The function returns only at EOF with ilevel <= 0; the exit paths above do not return. eval, inspect and the output helpers were not read.
note: usr.bin/m4/main.c:350-521 (quote 360-391 exit(1) at 382; EOF 442-454 exit(1) at 447, break at 450; internal stack overflow errx at 433 and 478). Reviewer round 15 right (stack overflow errx(1) has no warning/dump); reviewer round 1 right (fatal exits on unclosed quote/paren). In GNU-mimic mode an open call at final EOF just ends the loop.

name: mail1
prose: Sends the message on standard input to the recipients in hp (usr.bin/mail/send.c:282-414; returns nothing). It calls collect(); if that returns NULL it increments senderr and returns. In interactive mode it may prompt for Cc/Bcc or print EOT. If the collected file is empty and dontsendempty is set it jumps to out (message dropped silently); an empty body otherwise just prints a notice. It then sets senderr = 0 (so a collect failure count is reset only on this path), expands bcc/to/cc through usermap (NULL prints 'No recipients specified' and increments senderr), runs outof() (which can write to files named in recipients), and saves a dead letter with savedeadletter(mtf) if senderr is nonzero at that point. It elides the list; if no recipients remain it goes to out. With recordrecip it copies the original To name list; fixhead is applied, infix() builds the full message file and the function returns without closing the file if infix returned NULL (infix returns its input or the new file and never NULL, so that branch is not reachable). It builds the sendmail argument list; with debug set it prints the arguments and goes to out without delivering or recording. Otherwise it records the message with savemail (to a file named after the first recipient for recordrecip, or to the 'record' file), forks (on failure: warning, dead letter, out), and the child blocks several signals, uses the temp file as stdin and execv's sendmail (the 'sendmail' option or _PATH_SENDMAIL), calling _exit(1) if the exec fails; the parent waits for the child when 'verbose' is set, else calls free_child. At out it closes the message file with Fclose. The only path that returns without closing it is the NULL result of collect (no file) and the unreachable infix failure.

Reviewer round 1 right (debug/empty/no-recipient paths neither deliver nor record; the no-recipient case does save a dead letter via senderr); reviewer round 15 right (senderr not reset on the dontsendempty path).

name: image_init
prose: Initialises the image module (usr.bin/mkimg/image.c:734-755). It empties the chunk list (TAILQ_INIT), sets image_nchunks and image_swap_size to 0 and image_swap_pgsz to getpagesize(). It then calls atexit(image_cleanup); if that fails it returns errno (image_swap_file and image_swap_fd are not touched at that point). Otherwise it builds the template "<dir>/mkimg-XXXXXX" in the static image_swap_file buffer with snprintf, where dir is $TMPDIR (or _PATH_TMP if TMPDIR is unset or empty; a long path is truncated by snprintf), and calls mkstemp on it. If mkstemp fails (returns -1) it returns errno, leaving image_swap_fd at -1 (the atexit handler is already registered, and the handler later unlinks image_swap_file); on success mkstemp has replaced the XXXXXX in image_swap_file with the actual temporary file name and image_swap_fd holds the open descriptor, and it returns 0. The chunk list, counters and page size are set in all cases that reach line 745, that is all cases.
note: usr.bin/mkimg/image.c:734-755 (atexit 745-746, template 747-750, mkstemp 751-753); image_cleanup 708-732 unlinks image_swap_file and closes the fd. Reviewer round 15 right (mkstemp rewrites image_swap_file to the actual name on success); round 1 right about side effects, which the prose now lists.

name: parse_part
prose: Real name parse_part (static, usr.bin/mkimg/mkimg.c:247-329; mkimg_parse_spec does not exist). If spec is exactly "-" it increments nparts and returns 0 without allocating or touching partlist. Otherwise it callocs a struct part (ENOMEM and return if that fails), finds the first ':' in spec (EINVAL if none or if it is the first character), mallocs and copies the text before it as part->alias (ENOMEM on failure), and requires the character after the ':' to be ':' (size), '=' (file) or '-' (pipe), else EINVAL. The rest of the string is strdup'ed as part->contents (ENOMEM on failure; it may be empty). If the alias contains a '/', it is split there: an empty alias or empty label gives EINVAL, otherwise the label is strdup'ed (ENOMEM on failure). On success it sets part->index to the old nparts, appends the part to the tail of partlist, increments nparts and returns 0. On any failure after the part allocation it frees part->alias and the part and returns the error, so partlist and nparts are unchanged; part->contents (and the label if it had been allocated, which only matters for a failure that occurs after it) is not freed, so contents leaks when the later alias/label checks fail.

name: main
prose: Entry point of msgs (usr.bin/msgs/msgs.c:145-607; slice cut the head; ends with exit(0) at 606 and never returns). It drops privileges with setuid(getuid()) (err(1) on failure), handles SIGINT, and scans arguments: a leading digit gives the starting message, a digit in the second position a backward offset, otherwise it reads flag letters (c clean, only root or the daemon user else errx(1); f hush; h headers; l local; o; p pager; q query; s send; unknown letters call usage()). Unless send mode, the bounds file under _PATH_MSGS must be stat-able, otherwise err(errno) (or exit(1) with -f). It reads firstmsg/lastmsg from the bounds file and closes it. If cleaning or the bounds file could not be opened it rescans the _PATH_MSGS directory (err(errno) if it cannot be opened), computing first and last message numbers and, when cleaning, unlinking writable messages older than the cutoff, never lowering the old upper bound; unless send mode it then rewrites the bounds file (err(errno) if it cannot be opened). In send mode it opens the bounds file for writing and message lastmsg+1 for writing (err(errno) on failure), writes the new bounds, closes the bounds file (the new message file stays open until exit), copies stdin into the message (prompting for the Subject when stdin is a tty), and calls exit(ferror(stdin)) (or exit(1) when OBJECT is defined and no Subject was seen). With -c it then exit(0)s. For display it needs a non-empty HOME (else prints an error and exit(1)), reads and updates the .msgsrc next-message number, and loops over message numbers from firstmsg to lastmsg: it opens each message (skipping unreadable ones), prints the header lines, a line count, and in header mode only the headers; with -q it prints 'There are new messages.' and exit(0)s at the first (local, if -l) message; otherwise it reads the user's command (x exits 0; q prints '--Postponed--' and exits 0; others skip, replay or go to a numbered message) and updates the .msgsrc number as messages are passed; each message file is closed with fclose after processing. After the loop it may offer the last message again (with the 'o' flag on a tty), prints 'No new messages.' if nothing was shown and neither -f nor -q was given, and calls exit(0). The .msgsrc stream opened for update is not closed before exit.
note: usr.bin/msgs/msgs.c:145-607; stat of bounds 237-245, rescan 257-321, send mode 323-377, HOME 387-390, loop 453-584, end 589-606. Reviewer round 15 mostly right (bounds rewritten only if clean or no bounds file and not send; send mode writes firstmsg and nextmsg; a missing bounds file is fatal outside send mode, as stat fails first); round 17 right (fclose is called on bounds, message and the read-only msgsrc). name: main
prose: Entry point of netstat (usr.bin/netstat/main.c:241-621; slice cut the head). It calls xo_parse_args (exit(EXIT_FAILURE) on a negative result) and parses options with getopt, setting global flags; invalid fib numbers, unknown address families and unknown protocols call xo_errx(EX_DATAERR, ...), a missing jail option argument or bad interval calls usage(), 'Jail support is not compiled in' is EX_UNAVAILABLE. After options it takes an optional interval and wait argument, attaches to a named jail (EX_UNAVAILABLE if not found or the attach fails), sets live = no -N/-M, loads kvm symbols for non-live use, and rejects -x together with -T (EX_USAGE). Then the first matching report is produced and the program finishes with xo_finish and exit(EX_OK) (exit(EX_IOERR) via xo_err when xo_finish fails): -B (usage() unless live, bpf_stats), -m (mbpr; when not live it is called only if kread(0, NULL, 0) == 0, otherwise nothing is printed, still exit(EX_OK)), -Q (netisr_stats with the same kread condition), -i without -s (intpr), -r (route statistics with -s, else routepr), -o (nhops_print), -O (nexthop groups), -g (setfib, EX_DATAERR on failure, then multicast route stats or tables per address family), -p (one protocol via printproto), and otherwise all protocol tables for the selected address family via printproto plus unixpr when the family is unix or unspecified and -s is not set. The code never returns from main; every path ends in exit or an exit-calling helper. The kvm-loading and routing branches (lines 462-465, 495-548) and the called report functions were not read in detail.

name: addgroup
prose: Switches the process to the group named or numbered by grpname, keeping the old effective gid as a supplementary group (usr.bin/newgrp/newgrp.c:145-243; pwd is the file-static passwd entry). It saves egid, looks grpname up with getgrnam, else as a positive decimal id with getgrgid; if neither works it warns 'bad group name' and returns with nothing changed. The user counts as a member when pwd->pw_gid equals the group's gid or the name is in gr_mem. A non-member, if the group has a non-empty password and getuid() != 0, is prompted with getpass: a NULL result returns silently (no message), a NULL crypt result or a mismatch prints 'Sorry' and returns. It then mallocs sysconf(_SC_NGROUPS_MAX) gids (err(1) if malloc fails), calls getgroups (warning and cleanup/return on failure at label end), and, if the requested gid differs from egid and is in the list, removes it and calls setgroups under PRIV_START/PRIV_END (a failure warns and goes to end, skipping the setgid). It then calls setgid(grp->gr_gid) (warning and end on failure, so the gid is unchanged), and if the old egid is not in the list appends it with setgroups unless the list is full (prints 'too many groups') or setgroups fails (warning). Finally the buffer is freed (also at end) and the function returns nothing. Failures in the privilege helpers PRIV_START/PRIV_END may terminate the program (not read).

Reviewer round 2 right (setgroups/setgid failures warn and return; getgroups failure and removal-failure skip), round 15 right (getpass NULL returns without 'Sorry'), round 1 right (egid unchanged on password or setgid failure). Partly read: PRIV_START/PRIV_END definitions not inspected.

name: another_hunk
prose: Reads the next hunk from the patch file pfp (usr.bin/patch/pch.c:536-1203; slice cut the head) and stores it in the global arrays p_line/p_char/p_len in context-diff layout. It first frees the previous hunk's lines p_end down to 0, skipping the fake-copied range (p_bfake..p_efake, where p_end jumps to p_bfake) so shared lines are not freed twice, and resets p_efake. Then by diff_type: for a context diff it expects a line starting with '********' (otherwise next_intuit_at(line_beginning, p_input_line) and return false), reads lines up to the maximum hunk size, records the '***' and '---' header lines and line counts (malformed(), fatal() or grow_hunkmax() on bad numbers, hunks over MAXHUNKSIZE, duplicate or misplaced '---', or end of file; end of file or a premature '***'/'********' is accepted without fatal() only when the replacement part is absent and may be missing), and fills omitted old or new context lines from the other half; a diff of the old style may be re-labelled NEW_CONTEXT_DIFF. For a unified diff it reads the header (returning false after next_intuit_at if no valid '@@' header is found, malformed() on bad numbers) and the lines, where an end of file when fewer than three lines of space remain is treated as chopped blank lines and otherwise is fatal('unexpected end of file'). For a normal diff it reads the command line (next_intuit_at and return false if none), builds the '***'/'---' lines, and reads '<' and '>' lines, with fatal() on end of file or a wrong marker. When savestr runs out of memory (out_of_mem) it returns false after setting p_end to just before the failing entry (it frees partially built lines only in the unified branch); otherwise, if reverse is set it calls pch_swap and only prints 'Not enough memory to swap next hunk!' if that fails, stores a '^' stopper in p_char[p_end+1] when p_end + 1 < hunkmax, and returns true. Malformed input and truncated files normally end in malformed() or fatal(), which do not return. The unified and normal branches (lines 900-1180) were read only in outline.

Reviewer round 15 right (out_of_mem handling changes p_end and frees some lines); round 17 right (unified branch accepts end of file when p_max - fillnew < 3 at 972-976). Partly read: unified and normal branches.

name: create
prose: Subcommand 'create' (usr.bin/posixmqcontrol/posixmqcontrol.c:424-518; q_creation is passed by value). It builds an mq_attr from q_creation.depth and size and adds O_NONBLOCK to the open flags and the attribute flags when q_creation.block is false. It first tries mq_open(queue, flags) without O_CREAT; if that succeeds the queue exists (exists = true) and its depth and size are not changed. If it fails, it runs validate_size() and validate_depth() (which print their own warnings) and, only if both pass, clears set_mode and calls mq_open with O_CREAT, the requested mode and the attributes; if a validator fails no second open is made. If the handle is invalid it prints 'mq_open(create)' with warnc using errno as it is at that point (which the validators may have changed) and returns that errno. On FreeBSD builds only (__FreeBSD__): it obtains the descriptor with mq_getfd_np and does fstat (failure: warnc, mq_close, return the errno); if a user or group was given it applies fchown with the unset one taken from the stat result (for new and existing queues; failure: warnc, mq_close, return errno); and for an existing queue with set_mode set whose mode bits differ from the requested ones it applies fchmod (failure: warnc, mq_close, return errno). On other platforms those ownership and mode steps are compiled out. Finally it returns the value of mq_close(handle), which is 0 on success and -1 (not an errno value) if mq_close fails. It allocates nothing that it returns to the caller.
note: usr.bin/posixmqcontrol/posixmqcontrol.c:424-518 (first open 440-441, validators 448-453, open failure 456-461, FreeBSD block 463-515, return 517). Reviewer round 1 right (existing queue keeps depth/size); round 2 right (fchown on new and existing, FreeBSD only); round 15 right (the old prose contradicted itself on mode; fchmod only for existing queues). Prior prose said the final mq_close returns its errno; the code returns mq_close's own result (0 or -1).

name: inln
prose: Reads one input line (or one buffer-full of it) from inf into buf (usr.bin/pr/pr.c:1012-1104; slice cut the head). It reads characters with getc while a limit counter lim (decremented before each read) stays non-negative. When the global ingap (tab expansion width) is non-zero and the character equals inchar, the tab is replaced by spaces up to the next tab stop computed from the column *cps + characters already stored; if the expansion would not fit (col > lim) it first tries ungetc of the tab, and if ungetc fails it returns 1 immediately (that tab is consumed, *cps and *mor are not updated). If ungetc succeeds the function still writes spaces until lim is used up and then finishes as a too-long line, so the tab is read again by the next call. A newline ends the line without being stored. After the loop: if the last character read was EOF it sets *mor = 0 and *cps = 0 and returns -1 when nothing was stored, else the stored count; if it was a newline it sets *mor = 0, *cps = 0 and returns the count; otherwise (limit reached) with trnc set it reads and discards characters through the next newline or EOF and sets *cps = 0, *mor = 0, and with trnc zero it adds the count to *cps and sets *mor = 1. It returns the number of characters stored. With lim <= 0 the loop does not read at all (ch starts as EOF), so it returns -1 with *mor = *cps = 0, as if at EOF, without consuming input. Characters read are consumed except a tab pushed back by ungetc.
note: usr.bin/pr/pr.c:1012-1104 (ch initialised to EOF at 1017, gap loop 1027-1054, ungetc/return 1 at 1041-1042, EOF 1066-1072, newline 1073-1080, trnc 1085-1101). Reviewer round 15 half right: ch is initialised to EOF so it is not uninitialised, but lim = 0 is treated like EOF (returns -1), which the old prose did not mention. Old prose also omitted that spaces are still written after a successful ungetc.

name: setup
prose: Real name setup (static, usr.bin/pr/pr.c:1589-1849; the slice is only its tail). It parses pr's options and sets the global layout variables, returning 1 on failure and 0 on success. If stdout is a tty it tries to defer diagnostics into a tmpfile() stream stored in err; if tmpfile fails it sets err to stderr, prints 'Cannot defer diagnostic messages' to stderr and returns 1; otherwise err is stderr. egetopt then handles the page number (+), columns (-#, a value below 1 returns 1), -a, -d, -e, -F, -f, -h, -i, -L, -l, -m, -n, -o, -p, -r, -s, -t, -w and an unknown option (return 1); most invalid values print a message to err and return 1, and the unknown-option case returns 1 without a message. After options it defaults the column count (taking it from the number of operands with -m, or CLCNT), rejects -a with a single column and -a with -m, sets the default page width, defaults the tab characters and gaps when -m or multiple columns are used, rejects -m with multiple columns, computes the column width and page width (a column width below 1 prints 'page width is too small' and returns 1), and defaults lines to LINES. If lines <= HEADLEN + TAILLEN it increments nohead, else if nohead is zero it subtracts the header and trailer length from lines. For double spacing, lines == 1 clears dspace; otherwise addone is incremented when lines is odd and lines is halved. It sets the LC_TIME locale from -L or the environment, sets d_first from the locale's day/month order and sets timefrmt to a strdup of the day-first or month-first format (the strdup result is not checked) and returns 0.

Reviewer round 17 right: lines is reduced only when nohead is false and lines is longer than the header (1825-1828) and addone is incremented for odd lines under dspace (1837-1838). name: mulmod
prose: Static helper (usr.bin/primes/spsp.c:33-52) computing a * b mod n for unsigned 64-bit a, b and n with n > 0, using binary double-and-add so the product is never formed in a wider type. It starts with x = 0 and an = a % n, and loops while b is non-zero: if the low bit of b is set it adds an to x, subtracting n if the sum wrapped around or reached n (so x stays below n); it then doubles an modulo n (using wraparound-aware subtraction when an + an overflows 64 bits or is >= n) and shifts b right. It returns x, which is in [0, n-1] and equals the product of a and b reduced modulo n computed on the unsigned values. n == 0 is not allowed (a % n would divide by zero). It reads no globals and writes no memory.
note: usr.bin/primes/spsp.c:33-52 (loop 38-48, return 50). The old contract was reported false by random testing only for operands passed as negative signed values; the mathematical claim holds for unsigned inputs, but the contract field is left empty because the test harness and the unsigned semantics do not agree (cannot be sure of the signed interpretation).

name: main
prose: Entry point of renice (usr.bin/renice/renice.c:55-123; slice cut the head). It walks the arguments in order. Before a '--' delimiter, the arguments -g, -u and -p change the target kind (process group, user, process) and -- sets the delimiter; these can appear at any position before the delimiter, including between targets and after the priority. '-n' (once, only before the priority, and needing a following argument, else usage(), which exits 1) marks the priority as an increment and then the next argument is read as the priority. The first other argument is the priority, parsed with getnum; a priority that is not an integer or is out of range prints a message and makes main return 1 immediately (exit status 1, remaining arguments unprocessed). Each later argument is a target: for -u it is looked up with getpwnam and otherwise parsed as a numeric uid; for the other kinds it is parsed as a number; a parse failure or a negative value prints a message, increments errs and skips donice. For each valid target it calls donice, which reads the current priority with getpriority, applies the increment if requested, clamps to PRIO_MIN..PRIO_MAX, calls setpriority and prints old and new priority to stderr; a getpriority or setpriority failure warns and counts as an error. When all arguments are consumed, if no priority was given it calls usage() (exit 1); otherwise it calls exit(errs != 0), so status 0 only when no target errored and status 1 otherwise. name: split1
prose: Splits the input descriptor ifd into output files of bytecnt bytes each (usr.bin/split/split.c:210-266). It does not return: it loops on read(ifd, bfr, sizeof bfr) and ends the process with exit(0) when read returns 0, or err(EX_IOERR, "read") when read returns a negative value; every short or failed write also calls err(EX_IOERR, "write"). Per chunk read: if no output file is open (file_open is 0) and chunks is 0 or the local count nfiles (a local counter, starting at 0) is below chunks, it calls newfile() and increments nfiles. If the data would complete the current file (bcnt + len >= bytecnt) it writes the bytes needed to fill it, then writes each further whole bytecnt-sized block, calling newfile() before each when chunks is 0 or nfiles < chunks (otherwise the block is written to the current output file), then writes any remaining partial block, again after newfile() when allowed, or sets file_open to 0 when the remainder is exactly zero, and sets bcnt to the remainder. Otherwise it writes the whole read to the current file and adds len to bcnt. Once chunks files have been created no more are opened and further data is appended to the last output file (ofd). The globals bytecnt, chunks, ifd, ofd and file_open are used; newfile() was not read in full (it closes the previous file and opens the next name, exiting on error).

name: main
prose: Entry point of su (usr.bin/su/su.c:136-546; slice cut the head). Options: -f, -l, -m, -s, -c class; any other option calls usage(). The target user defaults to "root" (so a missing user argument is not a usage error) and is argv[optind] when present; the 'user == NULL' usage() test cannot trigger. It runs PAM for the target: pam_start (failure: syslog and errx(1)), sets PAM_RUSER and PAM_TTY, pam_authenticate (failure: syslog 'BAD SU' and errx(1, "Sorry")), re-reads the user from PAM, looks it up with getpwnam (errx(1, "unknown login") if absent), and pam_acct_mgmt (an expired token leads to pam_chauthtok; any other failure is errx(1, "Sorry")). It selects the login class (-c only for a real uid of 0, unknown class errx(1)), checks the shell for -m when not root, chooses the shell and csh-ness, restores the priority, calls setusercontext for the group (err(1) on failure), pam_setcred (errx(1) on failure) and, for -l, pam_open_session (errx(1) on failure). It then ignores SIGINT/SIGQUIT/SIGPIPE, creates a pipe (err(1) on failure) and forks (err(1) after PAM_END on failure). The parent waits for the child (handling stop/continue), then calls PAM_END and exit(WEXITSTATUS(status)), with err(1) if waitpid fails. The child waits for the parent via the pipe, restores signals, calls setusercontext for the rest (err(1) on failure), builds the environment (for -l it replaces the environment and chdirs to the home directory, errx(1, "no directory") if that fails), logs the su to syslog for a non-root caller, and execv's the shell; if execv returns it calls err(1). prose: Handles a systat command for the iolat display (usr.bin/systat/iolat.c:328-350; args is unused). name: keyboard_dispatch
prose: Processes one character typed on the systat command line (usr.bin/systat/keyboard.c:116-176) using the globals col (cursor position in the line buffer) and line. If ch == ERR it returns 0 when errno == EINTR and otherwise calls exit(1). A letter A-Z is lowercased. If col == 0: CTRL-L redraws the screen (wrefresh(curscr)) and returns 0, CTRL-G calls status() and returns 0, any character other than ':' returns 0, and ':' clears the command line and continues. Then, in order: if ch == erasechar() and col > 0, it returns 0 with no change when col == 1 and line[0] == ':', else decrements col, clears from col to the end of the line and returns 0. If ch == CTRL-W and col > 0 (tested before the kill character, so it applies even when killchar() is CTRL-W), it moves col back over trailing blanks and then over the preceding word; if that scan reaches index 0 while line[0] == ':' it returns 1 immediately with col at 0 and the screen unchanged, otherwise it clears from the new col and returns 0. If ch == killchar() and col > 0 it sets col to 0 (or 1 if line[0] == ':'), clears the rest of the line and returns 0. A printable character or space is stored at line[col] (no bounds check here) and echoed, and col is incremented. Finally it returns 0 if col == 0 or ch is not CR or LF, and returns 1 for CR or LF when col > 0 (the character itself is not stored). The caller treats a return of 1 as 'command complete' and runs the command in line + 1.

name: follow
prose: Implements 'tail -f/-F' (usr.bin/tail/forward.c:305-433). First, for each entry in files whose fp is non-NULL it marks active, prints the file name header when -v is set (or when more than one file is given and -q is not), and calls forward() to print the initial tail. If -F is not set and no file is active it returns immediately; this is the only return. Otherwise it sets last to the final entry, creates a kqueue (err(1) on failure), mallocs the kevent array (err(1) on failure) and calls set_events, which registers read (and, for -F, delete/rename) events on each open file, and which switches action to USE_SLEEP instead of failing when a file is on a non-local filesystem or when its kevent registration call fails. Then it loops forever: with -F it reopens files whose fp is NULL and checks the others (a file that cannot be reopened or stat'ed is shown, closed and counted as a change; a different inode/device or zero link count means the old file is shown to its end, closed and replaced by the new one), then it calls show() on every open file (a read error closes it and counts as a change), re-runs set_events when anything changed, and waits: in kqueue mode kevent() is called with a one-second timeout when -F is set (without a timeout otherwise), retried while it fails with EINTR and err(1) on other errors, with an lseek to the end if a read event reports negative data (a seek failure reports an error and continues); in sleep mode it usleeps 250000 microseconds. It never exits the loop normally; forward() (read in part) can itself call exit(1).

name: cour_dialer
prose: Dials a number on a Telebit Courier modem (usr.bin/tip/libacu/courier.c:59-113; num and acu are strings, the modem descriptor is the global FD). It sets HUPCL on the tty, then calls coursync(); if that fails it prints 'can't synchronize with courier' (and logs it when ACULOG is defined) and returns 0. It writes "AT E0\r", sleeps one second, flushes the tty and writes the configuration string; if cour_swallow("\r\nOK\r\n") fails (a mismatching reply or a timeout, in which case dialtimeout may be set by the alarm handler) it goes to the same 'can't synchronize' path and returns 0 without calling cour_disconnect. Otherwise it writes "AT D", replaces every '=' in num with ',' in place (modifying the caller's string), writes num and a carriage return, and sets connected = cour_connect(). If dialtimeout is then non-zero (a timeout during the connect wait) it logs it when ACULOG is defined and calls cour_disconnect(), which pulses DTR, resets the modem and closes FD. It returns connected: 1 only when cour_connect returned 1, and 0 when it returned 0 for any reason (timeout, read error, non-CONNECT line, CONNECT with an unknown baud suffix, overlong line).

name: cour_connect
prose: Waits for the modem's connect result after dialing (static, usr.bin/tip/libacu/courier.c:188-255). It first calls cour_swallow("\r\n"); if that fails it returns 0 at once (without printing; the SIGALRM handler is whatever cour_swallow left, which is SIG_DFL after a mismatch and the previous handler after a timeout). Otherwise it installs the cour_connect SIGALRM handler and, at label again, clears the 64-byte line buffer and dialtimeout and reads up to 63 characters, one per read(), each with an alarm of DIALTIMEOUT seconds. A timeout (handler longjmp), a read returning <= 0, or filling the buffer ends the loop. A '\r' ends the line: it calls cour_swallow("\n") (break if that fails); an empty line goes back to again; a line equal to "RINGING" goes back to again when VERBOSE is set (otherwise it is treated as a non-CONNECT line and ends the loop); a line not starting with CONNECT ends the loop; for a line starting with CONNECT it compares the rest with the baud table ("", " 1200", " 2400", " 9600", " 9600/ARQ") and on a match sets the tty input and output speed to that baud rate, restores the previous SIGALRM handler and returns 1. After a loop exit other than that match (including an unknown suffix) it prints the accumulated dialer_buf line, restores the previous SIGALRM handler and returns 0.

Where TIOCMSET is defined, with df03 and a saved speed other than B1200, it restores the saved speed on input and output. It returns 1 if c == 'A', else 0. name: hay_sync
prose: Tries to synchronise with a Hayes modem on the global descriptor FD (static, usr.bin/tip/libacu/hayes.c:288-312). It loops with retry++ <= MAXRETRY, i.e. at most MAXRETRY+1 attempts. Each attempt writes "AT\r", sleeps one second, asks FIONREAD how many bytes are waiting (the ioctl result is not checked, so len is uninitialised if it fails), and, if len is non-zero, reads min(len, DUMBUFLEN) bytes into the global dumbuf (the read result is stored in len and not checked, and no terminating NUL is added). If strchr finds '0' in dumbuf, or finds both 'O' and 'K', it returns 1 at once. With DEBUG defined it then stores a NUL at dumbuf[len] (out of range if len == DUMBUFLEN or -1) and prints the buffer. At the end of every attempt that did not return (including the last) it clears and sets DTR with TIOCCDTR and TIOCSDTR. If no attempt succeeded it prints "Cannot synchronize with hayes..." and returns 0. The strchr scan relies on dumbuf being NUL-terminated, which is not guaranteed when a read fills it or when stale bytes remain; no memory is allocated or released.

name: t3000_sync
prose: Tries to bring a Telebit T3000 modem on the global descriptor FD into sync (static, usr.bin/tip/libacu/t3000.c:276-319). It loops while already++ < MAXRETRY, so at most MAXRETRY iterations (none if MAXRETRY <= 0). Each iteration flushes the tty, writes "\rAT Z\r" with t3000_write (one byte at a time with 50 ms naps), zeroes the 40-byte local buf, sleeps two seconds and calls FIONREAD (result not checked), setting len to 1 if it is 0, so a read of up to sizeof(buf) bytes is always attempted; read's result is assigned to len and not checked. If strchr finds '0' in buf, or finds both 'O' and 'K', it returns 1 immediately, without executing the rest of the iteration. Otherwise it sleeps one second, writes "+++", sleeps, clears DTR (TIOCCDTR), sleeps and sets DTR (TIOCSDTR), then starts the next iteration. If the loop ends without success it writes a final "\rAT Z\r" and returns 0. The scan relies on buf being NUL-terminated, which holds only when fewer than 40 bytes were read, and with DEBUG defined buf[len] is written (out of range if len is 40 or -1). It leaves FD open and allocates nothing.

name: con
prose: Makes the tip connection (usr.bin/tip/tip/acu.c:58-152; returns a string describing an error, or NOSTR for success; all returned strings are literals). If DU is false (a direct line) it writes CM to FD when CM is set, logs 'call completed' and returns NOSTR without touching conflag. Otherwise it installs acuabort for SIGINT and SIGQUIT and sets a setjmp point; if an interrupt arrives later it ignores both signals, prints and logs 'call aborted', and, when the static acu is not NOACU, turns VERBOSE off and calls disconnect(NOSTR) if conflag is true or the dialer's acu_abort otherwise, then returns "interrupt". It looks up the ACU type AT in acutable: if it is not found it returns "unknown ACU type" (the SIGINT/SIGQUIT handlers stay installed). With a PN not starting with '@' it splits the comma-separated numbers, skipping empty ones, and for each calls the dialer (*acu_dialer)(number, CU), assigning the result to conflag and stopping on a true result, else logging 'call failed' and counting the attempt in tried. With PN starting with '@' it opens the phone file PH (printing the file name and returning "can't open phone number file" if that fails), reads lines whose first field equals HOST, and tries each non-empty number the same way, closing the file afterwards. After the loop: if conflag is true it writes CM when set, logs 'call completed' and returns NOSTR; else if no number was tried it logs and returns "missing phone number"; else it calls acu_abort and returns "call failed". conflag is a global that is assigned only from dialer results, so it is not reset on entry: if it was already true from an earlier call and no number was dialled, the function can return NOSTR (using phnum which may then be uninitialised in the log call) instead of "missing phone number".

name: transmit
prose: Sends the open file fp to the remote line (static, usr.bin/tip/tip/cmds.c:294-385). It signals the tipout process with SIGIOT, clears stop, installs stopsnd for SIGINT, sets the terminal to defchars and reads one byte from repdes[0] into ccc (a blocking read, result unchecked). If command is non-NULL it sends each of its characters, then with ECHOCHECK reads one byte back, else drains the line and sleeps five seconds. It then reads fp with getc, one logical line at a time: EOF or a stop request ends the transfer; a DEL (0177) is skipped unless RAWFTP; characters below space are filtered unless RAWFTP, with newline sent as carriage return (outside RAWFTP) and tabs optionally expanded to spaces (TABEXPAND, outside RAWFTP); lastc records the last accepted character. After each line, with VERBOSE it prints a line counter and with ECHOCHECK it arms alarm(ETIMEOUT) and waits for the PROMPT character, jumping to the end if the alarm sets timedout (printing 'timed out at eol') or a stop was requested. At the end (label out), if the last character recorded is not '\n' and RAWFTP is off (also when nothing was read) it sends a '\r', then it sends every character of eofchars when that is non-NULL, closes fp, restores the previous SIGINT handler, prints the transfer time with VERBOSE, writes the saved ccc byte to fildes[1] and restores the terminal settings (term). The routine returns nothing and does not report errors from send/read/write.

name: next
prose: Produces the next character of a tr string expansion (usr.bin/tr/str.c:55-130). It switches on s->state. EOS: returns 0. INFINITE: returns 1 without changing s->lastch, s->str, s->cnt or s->state (the caller keeps using lastch). NORMAL: looks at *s->str: a NUL byte sets state = EOS and returns 0; a backslash stores backslash(s, &is_octal) in s->lastch; a '[' tries bracket(s) (for [:class:], [=equiv=] or [c*n] forms) and, if it consumed a construct, returns next(s) recursively, otherwise (and for any other character) it decodes one multibyte character with mbrtowc into s->lastch and advances s->str (an invalid, incomplete or zero-length sequence calls errc(1, EILSEQ)); afterwards, if the following character is '-' and genrange succeeds the range state is set up and next(s) is returned recursively, else it returns 1. RANGE and SEQUENCE: when the repeat count is exhausted (cnt-- == 0) the state returns to NORMAL and next(s) is returned, otherwise RANGE increments s->lastch (SEQUENCE leaves it) and both return 1. CCLASS, CCLASS_UPPER and CCLASS_LOWER: increment cnt, take the next character of the class with nextwctype(lastch, cclass); if none (-1) the state returns to NORMAL and next(s) is returned, else lastch is set and 1 is returned. SET: takes the next entry of s->set at s->cnt++; OOBCH ends the set (state NORMAL, recursive next), else lastch is set and 1 is returned. Any other state value returns 0. The helpers genclass (errx(1) on an unknown class), genequiv, genrange (may malloc and err(1) on failure) and genseq (errx(1) in string1) can end the process, so it does not always return.

name: tsort
prose: Topologically sorts the global graph and prints node names (usr.bin/tsort/tsort.c:289-348; remove_node prints each name followed by a newline). While graph is non-NULL it repeatedly removes every node whose n_refcnt is 0 (remove_node prints the name, decrements the refcount of each successor and detaches the node), repeating until a pass removes nothing or the graph is empty; if the graph is empty it stops. Otherwise a cycle exists: the first time it counts the nodes and mallocs cycle_buf and longest_cycle of that many pointers (err(1, NULL) if either allocation fails). For each remaining node not flagged NF_ACYCLIC it calls find_cycle(n, n, 0, 0); a non-zero length means a cycle through n: unless quiet is set it prints 'cycle in data' and the node names of the longest cycle with warnx, and in all cases it removes n (printing its name) and clears the cycle marks and restarts the main loop; a zero length marks n NF_ACYCLIC. If the scan ends without finding any cycle (n == NULL) it calls errx(1, "internal error -- could not find cycle"). The function returns only when the graph has become empty, with all names printed once; cycles do not terminate it. remove_node's list unlinking (lines 361-365) and clear_cycle were not read in full.

name: cnt
prose: Counts one input for wc (static, usr.bin/wc/wc.c:202-351; slice cut the head). With file == NULL it uses descriptor 0 and the name stdin_filename; otherwise fileargs_open, and on failure it warns '<file>: open' via xo_warn and returns 1 (nothing to close). If words are wanted or multibyte counting is on in a multibyte locale it goes to the 'word' loop. Otherwise, when neither lines nor longest line are wanted it fstat's the descriptor (warn, close and return 1 on failure) and, for a regular file with st_size > 0, does not read it: it takes the character count from st_size, prints it with show_cnt, adds it to tcharct (unconditionally), closes the descriptor and returns 0. Otherwise (unstattable or empty/special file, or lines wanted) it reads the descriptor to EOF in blocks, counting characters and, if lines or longest line are wanted, newlines and the longest line; a read error warns '<file>: read', closes the descriptor and returns 1 with the running totals not yet updated; show_cnt is called during reading when siginfo is set. The 'word' loop reads to EOF, decoding multibyte characters with mbrtowc when applicable (an invalid sequence warns once per file via xo_warn with EILSEQ, resets the shift state and counts the byte as a character; an incomplete sequence at the end of a block breaks out of the inner loop), counting characters, lines, words (transitions from space to non-space using iswspace) and the longest line; a read error warns, closes and returns 1. On normal completion it adds to the totals (tlinect when doline, twordct when doword (word path), tcharct when dochar (non-word path) or dochar/domulti (word path), tlongline when larger), calls show_cnt, closes the descriptor (even if it is standard input) and returns 0. At the end of the word loop it can also warn once if a trailing incomplete multibyte sequence is found and no warning was given.

name: main
prose: Entry point of install(1) (usr.bin/xinstall/xinstall.c:163-419; slice cut the head). It parses options with getopt: -m uses setmode (errx(EX_USAGE) on an invalid mode), -l parses the link-type letters (errx(1) on an invalid letter), -N calls setup_getid (err(EX_OSERR) on failure), -U sets dounpriv, and an unknown option calls usage(). It then rejects -s together with -d or -l (usage()), frees the parsed mode set, honours DONTSTRIP, and calls usage() if no operands remain or only one is given without -d. It maps the -h digest name to a digest type (none, md5, rmd160, sha1, sha256, sha512; an unknown name warns and calls usage()). Unless dounpriv is set it resolves the group, owner and file flags: an unknown group or user that is not numeric calls errx(1), and an invalid flag string calls errx(EX_USAGE); with -U these three are skipped, so errors there cannot occur. If a metafile is named it opens it for append (a failure only produces a warning via warn), else digests are disabled. With -d it calls install_dir for each operand and exit(EX_OK). Otherwise the last operand is the target: if it exists as a directory then, with a symbolic link requested (-l s), it lstat's it (err(EX_OSERR) if that fails); if it is itself a symlink then argc must be 2 (otherwise errc(EX_CANTCREAT, ENOTDIR)) and the single source is installed over the symlink itself; in the other cases every operand but the last is installed into the directory (install() with the DIRECTORY flag) and it exits EX_OK. Otherwise exactly two operands are required (else a warning and usage()); when the target exists and no link is requested it stat's the source (err(EX_OSERR) on failure), requires the target to be a regular file (errc(EX_CANTCREAT, EFTYPE)) and rejects the same device and inode (errx(EX_USAGE)); finally it installs the file and calls exit(EX_OK). The function does not return. install(), install_dir and the digest code were not read here.

name: ac
prose: Reads the wtmp log named by file and accumulates connect time (usr.sbin/ac/ac.c:403-507). It opens the log itself with setutxdb(UTXDB_LOG, file), calling err(1, "%s", file) if that fails, and reads records with getutxent until NULL, then endutxent. For each record it copies usr->ut_tv into a local ut_timecopy and raises it to prev_secs if it is earlier (so ut_timecopy never goes backwards), updates prev_secs, and records the first time seen in FirstTime. With AC_D, when the local day-of-year changes it calls show_today with midnight of the new day. By record type: OLD_TIME stores clock_shift = ut_timecopy; NEW_TIME subtracts ut_timecopy from clock_shift (timersub) and shifts every current user's login time by clock_shift; BOOT_TIME and SHUTDOWN_TIME call log_out(usr) and set FirstTime = ut_timecopy; USER_PROCESS calls log_in(usr) unless the line is a pts/ line with an empty host; DEAD_PROCESS calls log_out(usr). log_in and log_out take the record itself, so they use the record's own, unclamped usr->ut_tv rather than ut_timecopy. After the loop it builds a fake SHUTDOWN_TIME record whose time is ut_timecopy with AC_W or the current time otherwise, prints the last day's total under AC_D when the day changed, and calls log_out on it to close all remaining sessions. Finally, with AC_D it calls show_today(now); otherwise it prints the per-user list when AC_P is set and then always calls show("total", Total) (the grand total is not printed under AC_D). It returns nothing. If the log has no records, ut_timecopy is used uninitialised in the AC_W and AC_D paths.

name: audio_record
prose: Real name audio_record (usr.sbin/bhyve/audio.c:257-281; the packet name audio_read_full does not exist). It asserts that aud and buf are non-NULL, that aud->dir is false (a recording stream) and that aud->fd is not -1 (these assert calls disappear if NDEBUG is defined). It then calls read(fd, buf + total, count - total) in a loop until total reaches count. A read returning a negative value logs a debug message (which says 'write') and makes the function return -1 immediately, leaving a partial prefix in buf and errno from that read; a read returning 0 adds nothing to total, so the loop keeps calling read and never ends if the descriptor stays at end of file. When count is 0 no read is made. It returns 0 once exactly count bytes have been read. It allocates nothing and keeps no references to aud or buf.
